## Extension: Dynamic Political Effects of the China Shock

We extend the ADH local-labor-market design to presidential political outcomes. The outcome is the Republican two-party presidential vote margin, $(R_{ct}-D_{ct})/(R_{ct}+D_{ct})$, where $R_{ct}$ and $D_{ct}$ denote Republican and Democratic votes. We estimate weighted CZ-level event studies:

$$
Y_{ct} = \alpha_c + \lambda_t + \sum_{k \ne 1988} \beta_k E_c \mathbf{1}\{t=k\} + X_c^{\prime}\Gamma_t + \varepsilon_{ct}.
$$

Here $E_c$ is cumulative ADH import exposure over 1990–2007 in thousands of dollars per worker; $\alpha_c$ and $\lambda_t$ are CZ and election-year fixed effects, and $X_c^{\prime}\Gamma_t$ allows baseline characteristics to have year-specific associations with the outcome. Each $\beta_k$ measures the difference in the exposure–margin association in election year $k$ relative to the omitted 1988 election; it is not a new trade shock in year $k$. Estimation uses ADH analysis weights and CZ-clustered standard errors. We compare a minimal specification without interacted controls, core controls (initial manufacturing share, college-educated share, and foreign-born share), and full controls adding female employment share, routine-task intensity, and offshorability. Interacted controls are standardized for estimation.

A central measurement challenge is that electoral data are observed for counties whose boundaries change over time, while ADH exposure is measured for 1990 commuting zones. We therefore bridge county election returns to 1990 counties using the FTZ county crosswalks, aggregate counties to 1990 CZs using the Tolbert-Sizer/USDA crosswalk, and merge those outcomes to ADH exposure. Our preferred bridge uses FTZ M5 weights where available and M2 fallback weights where M5 is undefined or zero. We validate retained vote shares, document fallback counties, and compare the results to M6+fallback, pure M2, and M4+fallback. These checks probe geographic harmonization choices while holding the 1990 CZ definitions fixed; they do not test sensitivity to alternative local-labor-market boundaries [@footeKutzbachVilhuber2021].

The political event study relates observed ADH exposure to voting outcomes conditional on fixed effects and baseline controls; unlike ADH’s original labor-market instrumental-variables analysis, it does not instrument exposure in the main regression. ADH exposure has a shift-share structure, combining initial CZ industry composition with subsequent industry-level import growth. Shift-share identification can rely on exogenous initial industry shares or on exogenous industry-level shocks, but these are distinct assumptions [@goldsmithPinkhamSorkinSwift2020; @borusyakHullJaravel2025]. Neither is established by the observed-exposure political event study, which also requires assumptions about counterfactual political trends. In our diagnostics, the ADH instrument strongly predicts exposure, but exposure also correlates with baseline manufacturing intensity and routine-task concentration. First-stage strength does not establish instrument exogeneity or validate a causal interpretation of this political event study. @tbl-bartik-firststage reports first-stage estimates in the political-outcome sample.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bartik-firststage
#| tbl-cap: "First-stage diagnostics for ADH exposure."
fs <- read_csv(output_path("diagnostics", "bartik_first_stage_diagnostics.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    Specification = recode(spec, minimal = "Minimal", core_controls = "Core controls", full_controls = "Full controls"),
    Estimate = fmt_num(estimate, 3),
    `Std. error` = fmt_num(std.error, 3),
    `First-stage F` = fmt_num(first_stage_F_t2, 1),
    `N` = n_obs
  )
knitr::kable(fs, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr")
```

@fig-main-event-study presents the main event-study estimates. The preferred inference is CZ-clustered. Conley, Driscoll-Kraay, Newey-West, state-clustered, and two-way clustered alternatives are computed as diagnostics, but several spatial and two-way variance-covariance matrices are non-positive-definite or require numerical repair in this short election-year panel. We therefore state the conclusions cautiously and base the main figure on CZ-clustered confidence intervals.

![Event-study coefficients for ADH exposure and Republican presidential margin.](../output/figures/fig_event_study_rep_margin_main_specs_m5.pdf){#fig-main-event-study width=100%}

The estimates do not reject a joint null of zero pre-1988 exposure coefficients, although this does not establish parallel trends. In 2016 and 2020, the minimally controlled coefficients are positive (0.00837 and 0.00874), but fall to 0.00083 and 0.00024 with core controls and become slightly negative (-0.00121 and -0.00176) with full controls. These coefficients are changes in the Republican two-party margin per additional $1,000 of cumulative exposure per worker, relative to the 1988 association; the 2016 and 2020 full-control estimates are not statistically distinguishable from zero (CZ-clustered $p = 0.668$ and $p = 0.537$). Even the minimally controlled 2016 and 2020 estimates are imprecise. Thus, the apparent delayed positive association is not robust to baseline controls; the evidence does not establish a causal political shift. Attenuation may reflect pre-existing differences in local political trajectories, but it does not distinguish confounding from heterogeneous responses. This matters because @autorDornHansonMajlesi2020 document differing political responses to trade exposure across initially distinct communities and political outcomes; our average CZ-level margin estimates do not test those heterogeneous responses.

To examine related electoral outcomes descriptively, we consider Republican votes per 1990 population, Democratic votes per 1990 population, and two-party vote volume alongside the margin. @fig-alt-decomp shows that the margin pattern should not be interpreted mechanically as a simple increase in Republican votes. These outcomes describe different electoral margins and vote volumes, but cannot separately identify voter switching, participation, or migration mechanisms; ratios with fixed 1990 population are not contemporaneous turnout rates.

![Political-outcome decomposition across election years.](../output/figures/fig_alternative_political_outcome_decomposition.pdf){#fig-alt-decomp width=100%}

Finally, we examine whether the single 1990–2007 exposure measure masks important timing differences. The original ADH exposure measure aggregates the China shock over a long period, so an event-study coefficient for 2016 does not mean that a new trade shock occurs in 2016. It means that CZs with greater cumulative exposure by 2007 evolved differently by 2016. To make this interpretation more transparent, we split exposure into 1990–2000 and 2000–2007 components and include both components jointly. @fig-subperiod-exposure shows that the estimated relationship varies depending on which subperiod of import growth is emphasized. Pre-1988 coefficients in this exercise are placebo relationships with future exposure, while post-2008 coefficients describe how early- and late-shock exposure predict later political differences.

![Subperiod ADH exposure event study, with 1990–2000 and 2000–2007 exposure terms entered jointly.](../output/figures/fig_subperiod_exposure_event_study.pdf){#fig-subperiod-exposure width=100%}
